analysis.one_liner: Sends $100 billion in emergency rental aid, bans most evictions and foreclosures for 12 months, and expands bankruptcy protections.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 232-180 in late June 2020 with only Democrats in favor; the Senate never voted on it and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill was a pandemic housing rescue package. It authorized $100 billion in emergency rental assistance and a $75 billion Homeowner Assistance Fund, put a 12-month moratorium on evictions covering all tenants and on foreclosures covering all mortgages, made mortgage forbearance automatic for delinquent borrowers, and raised bankruptcy protections so homeowners could shield more home equity and stretch repayments. It also offered mortgage servicers and landlords federal liquidity and a shield from investor lawsuits to keep the forbearance system working. The House passed it in June 2020; the Senate never acted.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters behind on rent, homeowners facing foreclosure, people experiencing homelessness, and low-income households in public, rural, and supportive housing would get direct aid and protection from eviction or foreclosure. Mortgage servicers and rental property owners also benefit from access to low-cost loans and a safe harbor from investor lawsuits while they carry out the forbearance and eviction rules.

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes $100 billion for emergency rental assistance to help people with rent, back rent, utility bills, and deposits, targeted to households below 80% of area median income.
Bans eviction filings for nonpayment for 12 months for all tenants, replacing a CARES Act moratorium that covered only tenants in federally assisted properties.
Bans foreclosures for 12 months on all mortgages, not just federally backed ones, and grants automatic 60-day forbearance to borrowers who fall 60 days delinquent, extendable to 12 months.
Creates a $75 billion Homeowner Assistance Fund, with at least 60% of each state's share reserved for homeowners at or below 80% of area median income, to prevent mortgage defaults and foreclosures.

Raises the bankruptcy homestead exemption from $15,000 to $100,000, expands eligibility for Chapter 13 bankruptcy, and lets homeowners behind on mortgages because of the pandemic cure defaults over up to seven years.
Adds funding for public housing, Section 8 vouchers, supportive housing for the elderly and people with disabilities, rural rental assistance, and homeless assistance programs.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the roughly $175 billion-plus in new spending. Landlords and mortgage servicers would absorb missed rent and payments during the moratoriums, though the bill partially offsets this with Federal Reserve loans and safe-harbor protections. Mortgage creditors would lose some of their claims in bankruptcy as debtors shield more home equity.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes a very large amount of new spending — $100 billion in rental assistance, $75 billion for the Homeowner Assistance Fund, plus billions more for housing programs — adding to federal borrowing during an emergency.

A 12-month ban on eviction filings for nonpayment applies to every tenant in the country, so landlords absorb unpaid rent; the bill partly compensates them through a Federal Reserve credit facility, but only if they agree not to evict tenants for nonpayment while the loan is outstanding.

The bill gives mortgage servicers a safe harbor from investor lawsuits over forbearance and loss mitigation, meaning investors in mortgage-backed securities bear much of the cost of payment suspensions.

Raising the homestead exemption from $15,000 to $100,000 lets bankruptcy debtors shield far more home equity from creditors, a real cost to lenders and an objection consumer-credit interests would raise.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and targeted: aid concentrates on households at or below 80% of area median income, and the eviction and foreclosure bans apply to everyone at risk of losing a home during a pandemic. The costs are also large — well over $175 billion in authorized spending plus burdens shifted to landlords, servicers, and creditors — but the bill deliberately cushions landlords and servicers with liquidity and legal protection. On balance the help to housing stability outweighs the costs, though the blanket 12-month eviction ban imposed real losses on small landlords that the bill only partly repaid.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed the bill on June 29, 2020, but the Senate received it the next day and never took it up — no hearing, no floor vote — and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: The House considered the bill under a rule covering several pandemic-relief bills and passed it 232-180 on June 29, 2020, with 232 of 233 voting Democrats in favor and no Republicans in favor (178 Republicans voted no).

Before the vote, Rep. Bill Huizenga offered a motion to recommit with instructions — a last-chance Republican amendment attempt — which failed 191-219, with 178 of 197 Republicans in favor and all but 14 voting Democrats opposed.
The Senate received the bill on June 30, 2020; the record shows no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

The bill would have replaced the CARES Act's narrower eviction moratorium (covering only federally assisted properties) with a 12-month moratorium on eviction filings for all tenants, and extended foreclosure and forbearance protections to all mortgages rather than only federally backed ones.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the Senate never acted, renters and homeowners facing pandemic-era eviction or foreclosure did not get the nationwide 12-month protections, automatic forbearance, or the $100 billion in rental aid and $75 billion in homeowner relief this bill offered. The parties better off because it died are landlords and mortgage creditors, who avoided a blanket ban on eviction filings, a 12-month foreclosure moratorium on all mortgages, and bankruptcy rules letting debtors shield up to $100,000 of home equity.

sides.party_line_note: The votes split almost entirely by party: on final passage 232 of 233 Democrats voted yes while 0 of 197 Republicans did, and the failed motion to recommit drew 178 Republican yeas against 218 Democratic noes and 1 Independent no.

industries.note: Servicers would have been required to grant forbearance to any delinquent borrower — on all mortgages, not just federally backed ones — and could not charge fees or report the forbearance adversely. In exchange, the bill directs the Treasury to give servicers access to federal liquidity programs and grants them a safe harbor from investor lawsuits over forbearance, so their losses are largely passed to investors and the government.

A 12-month ban on eviction filings for nonpayment would leave landlords unpaid while tenants stayed in place, and landlords receiving forbearance could not charge late fees or evict for nonpayment. The bill offsets this with a Federal Reserve credit facility making low-cost loans to cover documented rent losses — but only for owners who agree not to evict for nonpayment while the loan is outstanding.

Raising the bankruptcy homestead exemption from $15,000 to $100,000, expanding Chapter 13 eligibility, and allowing seven-year cure periods would let struggling homeowners shield far more home equity and stretch repayment, reducing what creditors can collect.

The servicer safe harbor deems forbearance and loss mitigation to be standard industry practice and shields servicers and securitization parties from investor claims, meaning the cost of payment suspensions falls on the investors who own the loans rather than on servicers.
